title: Properties of Fluids
summary: ## Pressure in fluids

Pressure is force per unit area, P = F/A, measured in pascals (N/m²). At a depth h in a liquid, P = hρg (written hdg in the NIOS text). It depends on depth, density and g, but not on the shape of the vessel or the viscosity of the liquid. A barometer works on P = hρg.
Example: two thigh bones of 10 cm² each support 40 kg, so P = 400 N/(2 × 10⁻³ m²) = 2 × 10⁵ Pa.
## Pascal's law and buoyancy

Pascal's law: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished to every part of it. Hence F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, which is used in hydraulic lifts, jacks and brakes. With piston diameters of 30 cm and 2.5 cm, 50 kg wt lifts 50 × (30/2.5)² = 7200 kg wt.
Buoyancy (Archimedes): upthrust = weight of the fluid displaced. For a floating body, ρ_body/ρ_liquid = fraction of its volume immersed.
## Surface tension

Surface tension T is the force per unit length on an imaginary line in the liquid surface (N/m). It makes the surface behave like a stretched elastic membrane and tend to the minimum area, which is why drops are spherical and mercury droplets join together. It numerically equals the surface energy per unit area (J/m²). It decreases as temperature rises, and detergents reduce it.

The angle of contact θ is the angle between the liquid surface and the wall, measured inside the liquid. It is less than 90° for water on glass (rises, concave surface), greater than 90° for mercury (falls, convex surface), and 90° when the liquid neither rises nor falls.
Excess pressure: 2T/r inside a liquid drop or an air bubble in a liquid, and 4T/r inside a soap bubble (two surfaces). A smaller bubble has the larger pressure, so it shrinks into a bigger one.

Capillarity is the rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube: h = 2T cos θ/(rρg). It explains kerosene rising in a lamp wick and water rising in plants. In a tube shorter than h, the liquid reaches the top without overflowing. The weight of the raised column equals 2πrT = πDT.
## Viscosity

Viscosity is the fluid's internal friction that opposes relative motion between its layers: F = −ηA dv/dx. The coefficient η has unit N s/m² (Pa s, also called poiseuille) and dimensions ML⁻¹T⁻¹. Glycerine is more viscous than water. Viscosity brings a churned liquid to rest.
Stokes' law: F = 6πηrv for a sphere moving slowly through a fluid; it can be checked by dimensions.

Terminal velocity v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η, so v ∝ r². Raindrops and parachutists fall at a small terminal speed, which is why a parachute works. A sphere 8 times heavier has a radius twice as large and so falls 4 times faster.
Flow is streamline (laminar) below the critical velocity and turbulent above it. Reynolds number Re = ρvD/η is dimensionless: below about 2000 the flow is laminar, above about 3000 it is turbulent.
## Equation of continuity and Bernoulli's theorem
Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so the flow is faster where the tube is narrower. Halving the diameter makes the speed 4 times greater.
Bernoulli's theorem: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline. It follows from conservation of energy. Where the speed is greater, the pressure is lower.

Applications: the venturimeter (flow meter); the danger of standing near a fast train, since low pressure between you and the train pushes you towards it; the curving of a spinning ball (Magnus effect); aeroplane lift. Speed of efflux from a hole at depth h: v = √(2gh) (Torricelli).

vsa: What is Reynolds number? What is its significance?
Re = ρvD/η (density × speed × diameter ÷ viscosity), a dimensionless number. It decides the nature of flow: below about 2000 the flow is streamline, above about 3000 it is turbulent.

or: What is terminal velocity? Write its expression for a sphere.
The constant velocity a body finally reaches when falling through a fluid, when the viscous drag plus upthrust balance its weight. v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η.

vsa: Why is it dangerous to stand near the edge of a platform when a fast train passes?
The fast-moving air between the person and the train has low pressure (Bernoulli). The higher pressure behind the person pushes them towards the train.

Verify Stokes' law (F = 6πηrv) by dimensional analysis.

Let F = k ηᵃ rᵇ vᶜ.
[MLT⁻²] = [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]ᵃ[L]ᵇ[LT⁻¹]ᶜ.
M: a = 1. T: −a − c = −2 ⇒ c = 1. L: −a + b + c = 1 ⇒ b = 1.
So F = kηrv, with k = 6π found by experiment.

or: Obtain the terminal velocity of a sphere of radius r and density ρ falling through a fluid of viscosity η and density σ.

At terminal velocity, weight = upthrust + viscous drag:
(4/3)πr³ρg = (4/3)πr³σg + 6πηrv.
v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η.

sa: Explain (a) why a spinning tennis ball curves and (b) why a small ball falling through a viscous liquid reaches a constant velocity.

(a) Spin drags air round the ball, so air moves faster on one side. Lower pressure there (Bernoulli) gives a sideways force and the path curves (Magnus effect).
(b) The viscous drag 6πηrv grows with speed. When drag plus upthrust equal the weight, the net force is zero and the ball moves at a constant terminal velocity.
la: Define terminal velocity and derive its expression for a sphere falling through a viscous fluid. Explain why raindrops do not hurt and why a parachute works.

Terminal velocity is the constant velocity a body reaches when the net force on it becomes zero.
Forces on a sphere: weight (4/3)πr³ρg down; upthrust (4/3)πr³σg up; Stokes drag 6πηrv up.
At terminal velocity: (4/3)πr³(ρ − σ)g = 6πηrv ⇒ v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η.
Raindrops are small (v ∝ r²) and reach a low terminal speed, so they land gently.
A parachute has a large area, so the drag is large and the terminal speed small, giving a safe landing.
Define viscosity and the coefficient of viscosity. Give its unit and dimensions. Does the nature of flow depend on viscosity? Explain Reynolds number.

Viscosity is the property of a fluid that opposes relative motion between its layers.
Coefficient of viscosity η: the tangential force per unit area for unit velocity gradient, F = ηA dv/dx. Unit N s m⁻² (Pa s); dimensions [ML⁻¹T⁻¹]. Glycerine is more viscous than water.
Yes: Re = ρvD/η is a pure number. Greater viscosity gives a smaller Re and more stable streamline flow. Re < 2000 means laminar flow; Re > 3000 means turbulent; between is unstable.
State Bernoulli's theorem and describe the working of a venturimeter (flow meter).

Bernoulli: for steady flow of an ideal fluid, P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant along a streamline (conservation of energy).
A venturimeter is a horizontal tube with a narrow throat. By continuity A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, the speed is greater in the throat, so the pressure there is lower. A manometer measures the difference P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²).
From this, v₁ = A₂√[2(P₁ − P₂)/ρ(A₁² − A₂²)], and the rate of flow is A₁v₁.
